name: Yushan National Park
blurb: Taiwan's highest peaks: oak and hemlock forest, deer, bears and hawk-eagles.

tip.title: Thin the oak mast
tip.text: Oak acorns feed boar, squirrels, rodents and bears. Cut Oaks by 50% and watch those eaters, then the marten, weasel, hawk-eagle and bear that depend on them.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Sunlight drives growth from the warm lowland forests up to the cold alpine zone. Cloud and mist often cut it back on the slopes.

nodes.name: Monsoon and typhoon rain
nodes.desc: Heavy seasonal rain keeps the mountain forests wet and feeds the streams that carve the steep valleys.

nodes.name: Cold and winter snow
nodes.desc: High summits are cold, and snow can lie on the peaks in winter. Cold sets the upper limit of trees and shapes the subalpine shrubs and cane.

nodes.name: Fungi and soil microbes
nodes.desc: Break down fallen leaves, cones, wood and carcasses, returning nutrients to the mountain soil.

nodes.name: Chinese hemlock
nodes.desc: A conifer that dominates a mid-elevation forest belt in the park, roughly between 2,500 and 3,500 m. It shelters many forest animals.

nodes.name: Oaks
nodes.desc: Broadleaf oak forests cover the lower slopes. Their acorns are a fat-rich autumn food for bears, boar, squirrels and rodents.

nodes.name: Yushan rhododendron
nodes.desc: A Taiwanese rhododendron, a shrub of the high mountain zone, whose tough leaves form thickets near the treeline.

nodes.name: Yushan cane
nodes.desc: A hardy bamboo of the high mountains that forms dense grassy stands in the subalpine and alpine zone, an open ground-level food source for browsers.

nodes.name: Formosan sambar deer
nodes.desc: The largest native herbivore in Taiwan, a mountain subspecies of the sambar. It browses and grazes in forests and open slopes.

nodes.name: Formosan serow
nodes.desc: A goat-antelope of steep rock and forest that eats leaves, vines, ferns and ground herbs, and licks minerals from cliffs.

nodes.name: Formosan Reeves's muntjac
nodes.desc: A small forest deer that eats herbs, shoots, fruits, fungi and nuts. It is the most recorded mammal in the surrounding area.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: An omnivore that roots in forest soil for acorns, roots and invertebrates, and also takes carrion.

nodes.name: Formosan rock macaque
nodes.desc: Taiwan's only monkey, living in troops. It eats fruit, young leaves, buds and grass stems, plus insects, snails and bird eggs.

nodes.name: Pallas's squirrel
nodes.desc: A tree squirrel of forests below about 3,000 m that eats seeds, fruit, leaves and flowers, and is regular prey of forest raptors.

nodes.name: Giant flying squirrel
nodes.wiki: Red and white giant flying squirrel
nodes.desc: A large nocturnal glider that eats mostly nuts and fruit with some leaves and insects. It was the most common prey in a Taiwan hawk-eagle nest study.

nodes.name: Taiwan white-bellied rat
nodes.desc: A rodent of primary hemlock forest, recorded in Yushan National Park. Rodents like this are food for snakes and weasels.

nodes.name: Yellow-throated marten
nodes.desc: An omnivorous, agile marten that eats fruit, rodents, birds and young deer, including muntjac fawns and boar piglets.

nodes.name: Siberian weasel
nodes.desc: A small carnivore that preys mainly on rodents and scavenges kills of larger carnivores such as the yellow-throated marten.

nodes.name: Taiwan mountain pitviper
nodes.desc: A montane pitviper of southeast Asia and Taiwan. A GloBI record shows it feeding on a Taiwan forest rodent.

nodes.name: Formosan black bear
nodes.desc: Taiwan's largest land carnivore, mostly a plant eater that shifts from spring shoots to fruit to acorns, and also takes carrion and animals.

nodes.name: Mountain hawk-eagle
nodes.desc: A forest raptor that nests in the park. In a Taiwan nest study giant flying squirrels and Pallas's squirrels were its main prey.
